title: When to stop rolling
objectives: Find an optimal stopping rule by comparing the value of stopping and continuing.

screens.title: Two reds up
screens.prose: Two red and two black cards are shuffled and turned over one at a time. A red pays £1 and a black costs £1. You may stop at any moment and keep your total.

state.caption: Each pill shows the reds and blacks left. Up is a red card (+£1), down a black (−£1).

screens.question: You have turned two reds, so you are up £2 with two blacks left. Stop or turn another card?

options.why: Only blacks are left. Each one costs £1 and nothing can win it back.
Turning a black loses £1 for certain, so stopping is strictly better.

hints.text: Turning can only lose, so stop.

feedback.correct: Stop: the cards left can only cost you.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what is left in the deck.

explain.text: With only blacks left, turning loses for sure, so the position is worth 0 more. That is the end of the game, where values are easy. We now work backwards from such positions.

screens.title: Work backwards
screens.prose: Let $V$ be the extra you expect to win from a position, playing well. Stopping adds 0. Turning adds the card's £1 or −£1 plus the $V$ you land in. So $V = \max(0, \text{turning})$. This is **backward induction**.

state.caption: Each pill shows the reds and blacks left. Up is a red card (+£1), down a black (−£1).

screens.question: Fill in the values, from the end of the game back to the start. Give fractions as decimals.

hints.text: From 1R 0B the last red is worth 1; from 0R 1B you stop, worth 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each value uses the ones nearer the end.

byKey.r0c1: From 1R 1B, a red wins £1 and you stop. A black costs £1, then the last red wins it back. So $\tfrac12(1) + \tfrac12(-1 + 1) = \tfrac12$.
byKey.r1c1: From 1R 2B: turning gives $\tfrac13(1 + 0) + \tfrac23(-1 + \tfrac12) = 0$, the same as stopping.

explain.text: The game is worth $\tfrac23$ of £1. Taking every card would be worth 0, so the option to stop is what has value. Each value came from positions one card later.

screens.title: Stop when ahead?
screens.prose: A new deck: three red and one black. Your first card is red, so you are up £1, with two reds and one black left.
screens.question: Stop now, or turn on?

options.text: Turn on: the rest is worth £$\tfrac43$ more

options.why: You stopped as soon as you were ahead. Two reds and one black are worth $\tfrac43$ more, which stopping throws away.

options.text: Turn one more card, then stop whatever it shows
options.why: A fixed plan ignores what the next card shows. After a black you should still turn the two reds left.

feedback.correct: Turn on. From 2R 1B the value is $\tfrac43$, more than stopping's 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare stopping with the value of 2R 1B from the table.

byKey.b: Stopping when ahead is the blurted rule. It gives up $\tfrac43$ here; in the 3-and-3 game it earns $\tfrac34$ against the best $\tfrac{17}{20}$.

explain.text: The money you hold is safe whatever you do, so only the cards left matter. From 2R 1B turning on is worth $\tfrac43$, so stopping costs that much. Stopping at the first gain gives the 3-and-3 game $\tfrac34$, short of its value $\tfrac{17}{20}$.

screens.title: Pig, alone
screens.prose: Pig for one player: roll a die and add the face to your turn total, $t$. A 1 wipes $t$ and ends the turn. Holding $t$, one more roll adds $\tfrac{2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6}{6} = \tfrac{20}{6}$ on average and risks $\tfrac{t}{6}$.

state.caption: Drag the point to the turn total where you start to hold.

screens.question: Drag the point to the turn total at which you should start to hold.

hints.text: Set the gain equal to the risk.
$t = 20$: roll below 20, hold at 20 or more.

feedback.correct: Hold at 20: below it a roll gains more than it risks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the gain $\tfrac{20}{6}$ equals the risk $\tfrac{t}{6}$.

byKey.early: You held too soon. Below 20, one more roll adds $\tfrac{20 - t}{6}$ on average.
byKey.late: You held too late. Above 20 the risk $\tfrac{t}{6}$ beats the gain $\tfrac{20}{6}$.

explain.text: One more roll changes $t$ by $\tfrac{20 - t}{6}$ on average, positive below 20. Rolling only makes $t$ larger, so once a roll stops paying it never pays again. That is why one roll of look-ahead finds the best rule.

screens.title: A harsher die
screens.prose: Same game, but now a 1 or a 2 wipes the turn. Holding $t$, a roll adds $\tfrac{3 + 4 + 5 + 6}{6} = 3$ on average and risks $\tfrac{2t}{6}$.

state.caption: Now a 1 or a 2 wipes the turn.

screens.question: Drag the point to the new holding total.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the gain 3 equal to the risk $\tfrac{t}{3}$.

byKey.old: That is close to the old threshold. Two wiping faces double the risk and cut the gain.
byKey.half: You halved 20. The gain also falls, from $\tfrac{20}{6}$ to 3.

explain.text: The gain is 3 and the risk $\tfrac{t}{3}$, so you hold at 9. A harsher die makes you cautious twice over: less to gain and more to lose.

screens.title: Three candidates
screens.prose: Three candidates arrive in random order, and you must accept or reject each on the spot. You want the best. Rule: let the first go, then take the first who beats them, or the last if none does.

state.caption: Candidates are ranked 1 to 3, and 3 is the best.

screens.question: What is the chance this rule picks the best candidate?

hints.text: Fill the "You take" column in your head.
In "3 then 1 then 2" nobody beats the first, so you take the last, 2.
The rule takes 3 in the orders 1 3 2, 2 1 3 and 2 3 1.

feedback.correct: It picks the best in 3 of 6 orders: $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out who the rule takes in each of the six orders.

byKey.third: That is taking the first, or picking at random. Letting one go first does better.
byKey.two-thirds: You counted every order where the best is not first. In "1 then 2 then 3" the rule takes the 2, which beats the 1, and misses the 3.

explain.text: The rule wins in 3 of the 6 orders, so $\tfrac12$, against $\tfrac13$ for taking anyone at once. With $n$ candidates, let about $n/e$ go and the chance of the best tends to $1/e \approx 0.37$. This is the **secretary problem**.

screens.title: Stop or go on
screens.prose: Every game here used one rule. A position is worth the larger of stopping now and going on: $$V = \max\big(\text{stop},\; E[\text{go on}]\big),$$ worked out from the end backwards. Graphs and DP valued its dice game this way: £4.25 for two rolls, £$\tfrac{14}{3}$ for three.
screens.question: In the card game, what is a position worth when no red cards are left?

options.text: Minus the number of blacks left
options.why: You may stop, so you never have to turn them.

options.text: It depends on your running total
options.why: The money you hold is safe. Only the cards left decide whether to go on.

feedback.correct: Going on can only lose, so you stop and $V = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare stopping with turning a black.

explain.text: When going on always has negative value, you stop at once and the position is worth 0. That is the edge case of $V = \max(\text{stop}, E[\text{go on}])$. Every value in the table was built up from such end positions.

screens.title: Why pig holds at 20
screens.prose: Put the threshold argument for pig in order, one justified line at a time.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Holding $t$, compare holding with one more roll.
A 1, chance $\tfrac16$, loses the $t$ you hold.
So one more roll changes the total by $\tfrac{20 - t}{6}$ on average.
That is positive while $t < 20$: roll below 20 and hold from 20.
Hold once your total beats your opponent's score.

hints.text: The risk and the gain come next, in either order.
Compare, risk, gain, net change, threshold.

feedback.correct: Compare, risk, gain, net change, threshold.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the risk and the gain before the net change.

byKey.d1: This game has one player. Only your turn total and the die matter.
byKey.left-out: All five true lines are part of the argument.
byKey.s5: The threshold comes from the net change, so it is the last line.

explain.text: The risk is $\tfrac{t}{6}$ and the gain $\tfrac{20}{6}$, so the net is $\tfrac{20 - t}{6}$. It changes sign at 20. In a two-player game the opponent's score would matter, but not here.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `card_game_value(r, b)`. It returns the value of the card game with `r` red and `b` black cards left, as a `Fraction`. Use the recursion you used by hand, with a memo so each position is solved once.
screens.question: Write the function.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests on small decks, all-red and all-black decks, and the full 26 and 26 deck. All but the last need an exact `Fraction`. The full deck has 729 positions, so it needs the memo.

hints.text: Base cases: no reds is 0, no blacks is $r$.
Otherwise take the max of 0 and the turning value.
`go = Fraction(r, r + b) * (1 + V(r - 1, b)) + Fraction(b, r + b) * (-1 + V(r, b - 1))`, then `max(Fraction(0), go)`.

feedback.correct: Backward induction in a few lines, exact for any deck.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: With 1R 1B, turning gives $\tfrac12(1 + V(0,1)) + \tfrac12(-1 + V(1,0)) = \tfrac12$. Check your two base cases.
byKey.test-4: With 1R 2B, turning is worth 0, so $V = \max(0, 0) = 0$. Return `Fraction(0)`, not a negative value.
byKey.test-9: The full deck needs the memo: without `@lru_cache` the recursion repeats positions billions of times.

explain.text: The memo keeps the 27 by 27 positions, so the full deck runs at once. Its value is about £2.62, more than the 0 of taking every card. Stopping well is worth over £2.60 on a fair deck.

screens.title: Taking profit
screens.prose: A position shows an open profit of £$t$. Each extra day you hold it, it gains £2,000 on average with chance 0.9. With chance 0.1 a gap through your stop gives back the whole open profit.
screens.question: Up to what open profit is holding one more day worth it, in £?

hints.text: This is pig with a different die.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the expected gain equal to the expected give-back.

byKey.even: That is the gain on a good day. The give-back grows with $t$, so solve $1800 = 0.1t$.
byKey.ninety: You compared £2,000 with $0.1t$. The gain comes only with chance 0.9: £1,800 a day.

explain.text: Holding adds $1800 - 0.1t$ a day on average, positive below £18,000. Above it, take profit. The edge and the stop-out chance set the threshold, just as the die did in pig.

ideas: Value a position as the larger of stopping now and the expected value of going on.
Work from the end backwards: end positions are easy, and each earlier one uses them.
When going on only gets riskier, a one-step check of gain against risk gives the threshold.

formula.name: Optimal stopping
formula.note: The 2-and-2 card game is worth $\tfrac23$; pig holds at 20.

summary.trap: Stopping as soon as you are ahead. In the card game it throws away the value of the cards still to come.

quiz.prose: The two-red, two-black card game, but now you must turn all four cards.
quiz.question: What is the game worth?

feedback.correct: 0: two reds and two blacks always net to £0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the four cards.

byKey.opt: That is the value when you may stop. Without the option, the cards net to 0.

explain.text: Taking every card always gives $2 - 2 = 0$. The game with stopping is worth $\tfrac23$, so the option to stop is worth exactly $\tfrac23$.

quiz.prose: Each roll of a fair die costs £4 and pays its face in £. You may stop whenever you like, before the first roll too.
quiz.question: What is the game worth?

feedback.correct: 0: each roll loses £0.50 on average, so you never roll.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare one roll's average payout with its cost.

byKey.one: That is one forced roll. You may refuse to roll at all.
byKey.face: You forgot the £4 cost of each roll.

explain.text: A roll pays 3.5 and costs 4, so it loses £0.50 on average every time. Going on always has negative value, so you stop at once and the game is worth 0. This is the edge case of the stopping rule.

quiz.prose: One-player pig, but now a 6 wipes the turn, and faces 1 to 5 add to it.
quiz.question: At what turn total should you start to hold?

feedback.correct: Hold at 15: the gain $\tfrac{15}{6}$ equals the risk $\tfrac{t}{6}$ there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the average gain of faces 1 to 5.

byKey.twenty: That is the usual game. Faces 1 to 5 add only $\tfrac{15}{6}$ on average.
byKey.five: You held at the highest safe face. Compare the average gain with the risk.

explain.text: The gain is $\tfrac{1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5}{6} = \tfrac{15}{6}$ and the risk $\tfrac{t}{6}$. They balance at $t = 15$.

quiz.prose: A hundred candidates arrive in random order, accepted or rejected on the spot. You want the very best.
quiz.question: Which rule does best, and roughly how often does it win?

options.text: Let about 37 go, then take the next best so far: wins about 37% of the time
Let the first half go, then take the next best so far: wins about 50%
options.why: With three candidates the chance was $\tfrac12$. With many it falls, and skipping about $n/e$ does better than half.

options.text: Take the first candidate: wins about 37%
options.why: Taking the first wins only one time in 100.

feedback.correct: Let about $n/e$ go; the chance of the best tends to $1/e \approx 0.37$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The best rule skips a fixed share of the candidates.

explain.text: Skipping $k$ and then taking the best so far wins with chance about $\tfrac{k}{n}\ln\tfrac{n}{k}$. That peaks at $k = n/e$ with value $1/e \approx 0.37$.
